verses.text: Sarah lived one hundred twenty-seven years. This was the length of Sarah’s life.
Sarah died in Kiriath Arba (also called Hebron), in the land of Canaan. Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her.
Abraham rose up from before his dead, and spoke to the children of Heth, saying,
“I am a stranger and a foreigner living with you. Give me a possession of a burying-place with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight.”
The children of Heth answered Abraham, saying to him,
“Hear us, my lord. You are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the best of our tombs. None of us will withhold from you his tomb. Bury your dead.”
Abraham rose up, and bowed himself to the people of the land, even to the children of Heth.
He talked with them, saying, “If you agree that I should bury my dead out of my sight, hear me, and entreat for me to Ephron the son of Zohar,
that he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which he has, which is in the end of his field. For the full price let him give it to me among you for a possession of a burying-place.”
Now Ephron was sitting in the middle of the children of Heth. Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of the children of Heth, even of all who went in at the gate of his city, saying,
“No, my lord, hear me. I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it. In the presence of the children of my people I give it to you. Bury your dead.”
Abraham bowed himself down before the people of the land.
He spoke to Ephron in the audience of the people of the land, saying, “But if you will, please hear me. I will give the price of the field. Take it from me, and I will bury my dead there.”
Ephron answered Abraham, saying to him,
“My lord, listen to me. What is a piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver  between me and you? Therefore bury your dead.”

Abraham listened to Ephron. Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver which he had named in the audience of the children of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver,  according to the current merchants’ standard.
So the field of Ephron, which was in Machpelah, which was before Mamre, the field, the cave which was in it, and all the trees that were in the field, that were in all of its borders, were deeded
to Abraham for a possession in the presence of the children of Heth, before all who went in at the gate of his city.
After this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre (that is, Hebron), in the land of Canaan.
The field, and the cave that is in it, were deeded to Abraham for a possession of a burying place by the children of Heth.

footnotes.content: I pause at the precision of the count: 127 years. The Lord numbers the days of His saints, and Sarah's long life came to its appointed end. Even the years of a faithful woman are written by the hand that gives them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There is no shame in the tears of a pilgrim. Abraham, who had so often trusted God for land, now weeps over the death of the wife who walked beside him in Canaan. Our faith does not deaden grief; it casts our grief upon the God who keeps every promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: How tender it is to see Abraham rise from before his dead. Love compels him not to sit in his sorrow forever, but to care for Sarah even in death. The same Lord who raised up Jesus will one day raise up all His own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham calls himself 'a stranger and a foreigner' among the Hittites, though he was rich in faith. This is the very identity of God's people: we are sojourners here, looking for a city whose builder and maker is God (Hebrews 11:9-10, 13-16).
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The children of Heth answer with courtesy to the man of faith. God often softens the hearts of strangers to show kindness to His pilgrims. Even in a land not yet his own, the God of promise goes before Abraham.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They call Abraham 'a prince of God' among them. What a testimony: a sojourner, not yet possessing a foot of land, is known as mighty before the Lord. The world's honor matters little when we are honored by our God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham bows himself to the people of the land. Faith does not puff him up with demands; it teaches him courtesy and humility. The man who argued with God for Sodom now humbly entreats strangers for a grave.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham does not ask for a favor in haste; he speaks plainly of his need. He wants to bury his dead 'out of my sight' — the ache of love that cannot bear to look on the face of separation. Our Lord knows that ache, and He will wipe every tear away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham fixes his eye on one specific cave: Machpelah, at the end of Ephron's field. He will not take charity for his own; he insists on buying it for the full price. A faithful man desires to own what God has promised, even if it's only a burial plot for now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The transaction happens at the gate of the city, before all the people. In that place of business and justice, Abraham secures his first legal foothold in the land of promise. God keeps His word in the slow, ordinary ways of witnesses and deeds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ephron offers the field and cave as a gift. It is a gracious gesture in the customs of the day. But Abraham knows the difference between a gift of courtesy and the certainty of a deed. Faith walks by promises, not by vague offers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again Abraham bows before the people. He will not argue or haggle like a grasping man; he honors those from whom he buys. The humility of the heir of promise puts the proud to shame.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham insists: 'I will give the price of the field. Take it from me.' He wants no cloud over his claim, no memory of debt. When God gives us an inheritance, we receive it as purchased by His grace, paid in full by our greater Abraham, Jesus Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ephron speaks again, pressing his offer in the hearing of witnesses. Both men are polite, but Abraham is resolved. Love for Sarah will not let him bury her by a vague loan of land; he needs it to be his by right.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four hundred shekels of silver — a substantial price. Ephron names it as nothing between friends, but Abraham takes him at his word. The man of faith pays full price for a handful of earth, because he trusts God will give him all the earth in the end (Romans 4:13).
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham weighs the silver 'according to the current merchants' standard' — careful, honest, above board. No trickery, no pressure. The heir of righteousness buys what God has promised with open hands and clean accounts. Our righteousness is not bought so, but freely given in Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The deed includes field, cave, and all the trees within its borders. God is faithful to give even the smallest details of His promise. What began as a word to Abraham now becomes a piece of land he can point to, though he still waits for the fullness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The purchase is made 'in the presence of the children of Heth, before all who went in at the gate of his city.' This legal transfer becomes the first title deed of the Promised Land in Abraham's hand — a pledge of the inheritance to come, guaranteed by the God who cannot lie.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At last Abraham lays Sarah to rest in the cave of Machpelah. After a lifetime of pilgrimage, she is buried in the land God promised. One day, the Last Adam will bring all His pilgrims home to rest and to rise in a land that will never be taken from them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo: a sojourner bought a burial plot to bury one he loved, pointing ahead to the day when the true Son of Abraham would buy us with His blood to give us an eternal inheritance. As of 2026-10, we rest in that purchase.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
